title: Tansy and Walnut's Moonlight Mishap
markdown:
When the moon was a peeled orange and long shadows lay like slumbering giants across Lily’s floor, Tansy and Walnut waited for the prearranged signal: contented snores.

Tansy was a squirrel with paws like a blur and a heart that beat faster when baking. She wanted, with a singular heat, to win the Annual Moonlight Baking Contest. Speed, she believed, was the crucial ingredient. Walnut was a teddy of considerable fluff and more considerable optimism, fur the colour of toasted marshmallows, button eyes in perpetual cheer. He was convinced there was always a shortcut.

Every day, while Lily was at school or lost in play, Tansy turned the shadowy oak hollow into a miniature culinary studio. She scattered fine acorn flour, measured crushed nuts with a tiny thimble, sighed dramatically, then nibbled, whiskers twitching with pride and impatience. A lopsided pinecone pastry cooled on a leaf plate and was declared almost ready, which in Tansy’s kitchen meant eat now. Walnut, meanwhile, dedicated sunbeams to his most dashing poses, dreaming of grand adventures and the most expeditious routes to reach them, a distinguished explorer who never left the safe confines of Lily’s bedspread and therefore never got lost, which he counted as skill.

Until one day, as Tansy frosted a lopsided batch of pinecone pastries, a rustle of leaves brought a secret to her ears: the contest would be held in the hazel copse beyond the cricket field. Excitement, then the familiar flutter. Walnut, eavesdropping from the sill, immediately invented the quickest path.

So when Lily’s breathing deepened, Tansy in a flour-dusted homemade apron and Walnut with jet-bright buttons slipped through the ajar window. Cool air: damp earth, sweet clover, wild mint. The aroma of adventure, Walnut declared, which Tansy translated as the aroma of being late if they dawdled.

“The hazel copse! I know a perfect shortcut,” Walnut announced, puffing until his fluff strained. “An old deer path. Those creatures never take the long way.”

Tansy clutched her basket of hazelnut swirls—hours of attempted uniformity, a few flatter than planned. “Lead the way. I trust you.”

They scurried across the dewy cricket field, where the moon hung like a luminous pearl and shadows played tag with anyone foolish enough to run. A late cricket offered one note and thought better of a second. Walnut, true to his word, found a faint track into the hushed woods, less a path than a suggestion, a whisper of where others had trod long ago. It wound through bramble that snagged Tansy’s bushy tail with a scratchy protest, under low-hanging branches that brushed their noses with a ticklish caress, over mossy humps that muffled footsteps in damp earth. Quiet, almost unnervingly. No contest chatter. No smell of other people’s tarts. The further they ventured, the more the faint track seemed decorated: tiny smooth pebbles in neat, almost artistic lines; small carved wooden figures, no bigger than Tansy’s paw, peeking from ferns as if they had been posted there to slow people down on purpose.

“A very ceremonial shortcut,” Tansy whispered, whiskers drooping. She had the unsettling sense they were heading not toward speed but toward a deliberate slowness.

Walnut pointed a stubby paw. “They must be preparing something important! The royal deer path! Special occasions!” He pictured a tiny crown.

The decorated track delivered them not to the friendly hazel copse but to a small ancient stone bridge. Moonlight, sharp and clear, striped the weathered wooden planks with velvet dark. A reverent silence hung so profound it felt like a blanket you were not meant to fold. Lichen spelled nothing helpful. A moth used the rail as a road. It was beautiful, the kind of place that asked for quiet contemplation and absolutely refused to be late for a contest. Clearly not a shortcut to pastry. They had taken the Woodland Procession, reserved for solemn ceremonies, meant for reflection, not hurried swirls and floury aprons. Somewhere a deer, if deer used this path at all, was taking its time.

Tansy’s heart sank like a stone dropped into a well that had not asked for pastry. She looked into the basket. Some of the precious swirls had jiggled and nudged on the unusual journey and now resembled sleepy clouds more than treats. She could hear the faint cheerful murmur of voices from the hazel copse. They were late, and the mint on the air no longer smelled like winning.

They arrived to a chorus of polite, slightly disappointed murmurs from assembled woodland creatures who had already done the sensible thing. Other participants had used well-trodden paths: a badger with perfectly formed blackberry tarts that gleamed like polished jewels; a busy family of field mice with charmingly miniature honey cakes stacked like tiny towers; a wise old owl with a magnificent moon-dusted seed cake that resembled a celestial map and did not appear to have travelled by procession. Tansy’s hazelnut swirls, by comparison, looked a trifle ruffled, a little squashed, as if they had attended a solemn ceremony against their will. Her flour-dusted apron suddenly felt like a badge of shame. She noticed the flicker of regret, a tiny shadow, in Walnut’s usually bright buttons. A field mouse coughed, kindly, into a crumb.

Bartholomew the hedgehog, spines impeccably neat, cleared his throat. Tansy wanted to burrow and vanish. She took a breath instead, paws trembling.

“We’re very sorry we’re late. My swirls got a bit squashed. Walnut thought he knew a shortcut. It was the Woodland Procession. Very pretty. Very peaceful. Very, very slow.”

Walnut did not blame the deer, the pebbles, or nature. “It was entirely my idea. I was so sure there was a quicker, cleverer way that I failed to ask if it was the right way. Or even a path.”

A hush. Tansy braced for a lecture on punctuality.

Bartholomew surveyed the disheveled swirls. He did not scowl. He leaned and sniffed with an appreciative twitch. “Honesty is often a delightful ingredient. And a journey shared, even a delayed one, is a journey well-made.” He took a small perfect bite. His eyes widened in pleasure. “Remarkable. Despite the unusual journey, the flavour is exquisite.” A wise rabbit and a discerning field mouse nodded. Warmth spread through Tansy’s chest, brighter than a ribbon.

After that night the oak hollow still smelled of acorn flour, but Tansy measured twice and let the swirls sit before she ran. Walnut still practised poses in the sunbeam, explorer of bedspreads, and when he proposed a deer path he also proposed asking a deer. They did not take first prize that night. They walked home across the cricket field with a lighter basket and two honest appetites, the peeled-orange moon keeping them company without offering a shorter way.
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing night-time woodland adventure for older children
